name: Orvietan

lead: Orvietan was a famous early-modern panacea, sold at fairs as an antidote to poisons, snakebite and plague. It was a mixture of many herbs and spices with honey and wine.

Its link to recovery and wellbeing is historical: it was marketed as a restorative and universal remedy, in the tradition of theriac. It is documented by historians of pharmacy, not as an appearance product.

paras: It was prepared as a liquid electuary or powder and sold by itinerant sellers and pharmacists, often with public demonstrations.

Recipes varied widely, and some contained partly toxic herbs; counterfeiting was common [2]. Historians describe theriac-type remedies, which often contained opium, as examples of polypharmacy that fell out of favor [3].

angle.text: Orvietan was promoted as a universal restorative. Its relevance is as historical context for tonics and recovery remedies, not as a current appearance method.

lead: Orvietan, or orviétan, was a remedy sold across Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries as a cure-all and antidote. It is credited to Gerolamo Ferranti, who performed at Paris fairs by swallowing poisons handed to him and then curing himself with it [1]. Other sellers included Jean Vitrario and Cristoforo Contugi [1].

Recipes published by Johann Schroder in 1655 and Moyse Charas in 1676 survive, and a study of 35 recipes found between 9 and 57 ingredients, among them angelica, wolfsbane, gentian, valerian, rue, cinnamon, viper meat, honey and white wine [1]. It appeared in works by Moliere, Voltaire and Balzac and was carried by explorers to New France [1][2].

paras: It was a liquid mixture of herbs, wine and honey, also sold as powder in lead boxes, and was thought to counter poisonings, snakebite, rabid-animal bites and plague [1]. Theriac itself stayed in the French pharmacopeia until 1908, and Orvietan is described as its most famous imitation, prompting pharmacists to prepare their own [3]. Historical reviews place Orvietan among the antidotes of classical antiquity and early modern Europe surveyed in snakebite research [4].
No studies found. Modern snakebite research draws on compounds from plants used in historical antidotes such as Orvietan [4].
